rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the overall elution window. This should reveal whether peaks are crowded early, late, or across the full range so later runs can trim the phi window and adjust slope.

All 10 peaks eluted well within the gradient and the last peak is far from the run limit, so trim the gradient window to the observed elution region to improve time efficiency while keeping similar slope. This probes whether we can preserve full resolution with a much shorter effective solvent range focused on the compounds.

The broad window was clearly better, so now test a steeper gradient at the same temperature to trade some resolution for a shorter run and see whether the critical mid-cluster pair is slope-sensitive. This establishes whether CRF can improve by compressing the already over-resolved separation.

The 10 min run is faster but over-compresses the central cluster, especially peaks 5–7, so move to an intermediate gradient time to recover resolution while keeping the time term near zero. This directly measures how slope-sensitive the critical pair is between 10 and 20 minutes.

Resolution of the critical 6/7 pair improved strongly from 10 to 14 minutes, so extend the gradient slightly further to target full resolution while likely retaining a zero time penalty. This should be near the optimum tradeoff between the 14 and 20 minute runs.

Slope optimization is already near-optimal, and the remaining issue is the tight 6/7 pair that may not respond much further to tG, so probe temperature for a selectivity change while keeping the best gradient time. Lowering T should modestly expand retention and may separate that close pair without introducing a time penalty.

Lower temperature hurt selectivity by collapsing peaks 5/6, so test the opposite direction at the current best tG. A modest increase to 45 C could reorder or open the central cluster while likely preserving the zero time penalty.

Temperature changes made the critical cluster worse, so return to 40 C and fine-tune gradient time above 16 minutes. Since the 6/7 pair improves with shallower slope, 18 minutes may keep full resolution while reducing the time penalty versus 20 minutes.

The optimum appears to lie between 10 and 16 minutes, and 14 minutes is currently best, so test the other side of that local maximum. This brackets the tG optimum more tightly and checks whether a slightly faster run can retain enough central-cluster resolution to beat the current CRF.

Keep the best tG and temperature, but slightly narrow the upper end of the gradient window since the last peak elutes far before the gradient ends. This subtly reduces effective slope in the peak region and may open the critical 6/7 pair without adding enough time to hurt the score.

Narrowing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the score, so continue in the same direction to further shallow the effective gradient around the crowded middle peaks. The last peak still has ample margin, so phi1 0.85 may increase the critical 6/7 resolution while keeping the run fast enough for no time penalty.

The best region is around phi1 0.90 and tG 14, but phi1 reduction improved selectivity while adding some retention, so now test a slightly steeper time program at that better solvent window. This checks whether we can keep the improved selectivity from phi1 0.90 while shortening the run enough to maintain or exceed the current best CRF.

The best solvent window is now clear, so test the adjacent shallower slope at the same phi range to see if the 6/7 pair gains enough resolution to offset any small time penalty. This is the most direct local refinement around the current best method.

The local optimum in slope/window is well mapped, and only selectivity of the central cluster remains limiting, so probe a stronger temperature change at the best phi window. Since 35 and 45 C both worsened separation, 30 C tests whether selectivity changes nonlinearly enough to improve the critical pair.

Large downward temperature shifts strongly worsened selectivity, so test the other extreme at the best solvent program to rule in or out a beneficial high-temperature reordering. This is the remaining major orthogonal lever that could still beat the current best if the critical pair responds nonlinearly.

Temperature is clearly not helping, so keep the best T and continue narrowing the upper gradient limit around the observed elution window. Since phi1 0.85 fully resolved all pairs but incurred only a small time penalty, phi1 0.80 may further improve central-cluster spacing enough to offset any extra retention.

The best chemistry remains 0.05–0.90 over 14 min at 40 C, but with nine injections left it is still worth checking the final untested temperature extreme for an unexpected selectivity improvement. If 25 C also degrades the central cluster, we can stop spending budget on temperature and focus entirely on local solvent-window refinements around the current optimum.

Temperature exploration is exhausted, so probe the remaining solvent-window dimension by slightly raising phi0 while keeping the current best phi1 and tG. The first peak is not near void, and increasing phi0 may redistribute gradient strength toward the crowded mid-cluster and improve the limiting 6/7 separation.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved CRF, so continue that trend while keeping the currently optimal upper window and slope. This tests whether a bit more front-end compression further redistributes selectivity into the crowded middle region without pushing the earliest peak too close to the void.

The current optimum is centered at phi0 0.10, and narrowing phi1 helped at lower phi0, so combine those two favorable directions. This should slightly shallow the useful gradient in the crowded region and may push the limiting 6/7 pair just enough while keeping the run comfortably in the zero-penalty zone.

We have reached CRF 1.000, so this is a confirmatory/local-mapping run around the optimum by combining the best phi1 with the next higher phi0 that previously performed well. It tests whether the optimum sits on a broader plateau or whether 0.10/0.85 is uniquely best, without risking truncation.

With two neighboring methods now at CRF 1.000, map the high-phi0 edge of this optimum plateau. This checks whether further increasing phi0 still preserves full score or starts to push the first peak toward unretained behavior and reduce robustness.

Map the lower-phi1 edge around the 1.000 plateau by tightening the upper solvent limit one more step while keeping the best phi0. This tests whether the optimum is broad toward a shallower effective gradient or whether extra retention starts to cost score again.

One final plateau-mapping check is to combine the second-best phi0 with the lower phi1 edge. This determines whether the CRF 1.000 region extends diagonally in phi0/phi1 space or whether the extra retention at phi1 0.80 consistently pushes the score down.

Use the final injection to complete the local phi0/phi1 map around the optimum plateau by testing the remaining adjacent corner. This confirms whether the 1.000 region extends toward higher phi0 at the wider upper window or falls off once the first peak approaches the void too closely.
